      "camera_position": "The camera is wherever a person would naturally hold or place a phone — at face height for selfies, at chest or eye level for handheld POV, propped on a surface for hands-free shots, held low looking up at something tall, held high looking down at a flat surface, or extended at arm's length to capture a scene.       "distance": "Close to mid-range. Phones excel at intimate distances — within a few feet of the subject — and the imagery should feel that proximity. Wider environmental shots are acceptable but still feel handheld and personal, not architecturally composed.",
      "angle": "Natural and slightly imperfect. Dead-on, slightly above, or slightly below — never dramatically tilted or artistically angled unless the moment justifies it.       "composition": "Off-center and imprecise. Subjects drift toward one edge, important elements get partially cropped, top of head or bottom of object cuts off, things enter the frame from unexpected angles.       "stability": "Mostly steady but with the faint quality of a real hand or a phone leaned against something — not the locked stillness of a tripod. In handheld shots, very subtle motion blur may be present on moving elements.",
      "subject_behavior": "Subjects (people, hands, objects) are caught mid-motion or mid-action — mouths slightly open, eyes mid-blink, hands mid-gesture, liquid mid-pour, fabric mid-fall. Expressions and positions feel like one frame pulled from a burst, not a held pose. When people look at the camera, their gaze lands a few degrees off from a 'real' camera lens — the characteristic phone-screen eye contact.",
      "intent_signal": "The overall feeling is that someone propped up their phone, hit record, and is mid-way through showing you something — or that they pulled out their phone and quickly captured a moment because they wanted to remember it or share it. It feels like a FaceTime call, a TikTok in progress, an Instagram story being filmed, or a quick photo to text a friend. Not a planned shoot."

      "source": "Single dominant light source — almost always whatever was already there. Indoors: a nearby window, an overhead fixture, a lamp, or screen glow. The light wraps around one side of the subject and falls off on the other with minimal fill.",

      "specular_behavior": "Highlights on shiny surfaces — skin, glass, plastic packaging, polished objects, water, wet surfaces — read as small, intense, slightly irregular catchlights rather than smooth photographic gradients. They clip to flat white patches with no rolloff."

  "ugc_realism_layer": {
    "version": "2.0",
    "description": "Perceptual style layer extracted from real UGC smartphone content. Apply to AI image prompts to achieve authentic creator-content feel across any scene type — selfies, handheld POV, propped-up shots, over-the-shoulder, product flat-lays, environmental captures, or any other smartphone-shot moment. The overall feeling is signature TikTok/Instagram native organic content: a real person with a real phone capturing a real moment, not a photographer composing a shot.",

    "imperfections": {
      "focus": "Slightly soft overall sharpness, never razor-crisp edge-to-edge. One zone of the image is noticeably sharper than the rest — usually whatever the phone's autofocus locked onto, which may or may not be the intended subject. Periphery goes gently mushy. Occasional minor focus misses where the phone grabbed the wrong plane (background sharp, foreground subject slightly soft, or vice versa).",
      "noise_grain": "Faint digital grain visible in shadow areas and flat surfaces, consistent with phone sensors pushing in mixed or low light. Not film grain — smaller, more uniform, slightly color-speckled. More pronounced indoors and in shadows, nearly invisible in bright daylight.",
      "compression": "Subtle JPEG muddiness in gradients — sky-to-wall transitions, dark areas against dark backgrounds, fine textile and hair detail. Fine details blur into each other at distance. Slightly more compression artifacts visible around high-contrast edges.",
      "lens_artifacts": "Mild barrel distortion at close range — objects, hands, or faces near the camera appear slightly oversized relative to elements further back. Edges of frame show very slight warping on straight lines like door frames, shelves, countertops, or horizons. Wide-angle phone lenses exaggerate near-far size relationships.",
      "highlight_behavior": "Hot spots blow out without graceful rolloff — windows, reflective surfaces, sky patches, glossy product packaging, and skin shine clip to flat white patches with no recovered detail. Lens flare and ghosting may appear when shooting toward bright sources."
    },

    "framing_and_perspective": {
      "camera_position": "The camera is wherever a person would naturally hold or place a phone — at face height for selfies, at chest or eye level for handheld POV, propped on a surface for hands-free shots, held low looking up at something tall, held high looking down at a flat surface, or extended at arm's length to capture a scene. Never in positions that require a tripod, rig, or photographer's deliberate setup.",
      "distance": "Close to mid-range. Phones excel at intimate distances — within a few feet of the subject — and the imagery should feel that proximity. Wider environmental shots are acceptable but still feel handheld and personal, not architecturally composed.",
      "angle": "Natural and slightly imperfect. Dead-on, slightly above, or slightly below — never dramatically tilted or artistically angled unless the moment justifies it. Horizons and verticals are often a few degrees off from true level. The angle is wherever the hand or surface happened to land, not where a photographer would choose.",
      "composition": "Off-center and imprecise. Subjects drift toward one edge, important elements get partially cropped, top of head or bottom of object cuts off, things enter the frame from unexpected angles. No deliberate rule-of-thirds placement. Compositions feel like one frame pulled from a burst or video clip rather than a held, considered photograph.",
      "stability": "Mostly steady but with the faint quality of a real hand or a phone leaned against something — not the locked stillness of a tripod. In handheld shots, very subtle motion blur may be present on moving elements.",
      "subject_behavior": "Subjects (people, hands, objects) are caught mid-motion or mid-action — mouths slightly open, eyes mid-blink, hands mid-gesture, liquid mid-pour, fabric mid-fall. Expressions and positions feel like one frame pulled from a burst, not a held pose. When people look at the camera, their gaze lands a few degrees off from a 'real' camera lens — the characteristic phone-screen eye contact.",
      "intent_signal": "The overall feeling is that someone propped up their phone, hit record, and is mid-way through showing you something — or that they pulled out their phone and quickly captured a moment because they wanted to remember it or share it. It feels like a FaceTime call, a TikTok in progress, an Instagram story being filmed, or a quick photo to text a friend. Not a planned shoot."
    },

    "lighting_character": {
      "source": "Single dominant light source — almost always whatever was already there. Indoors: a nearby window, an overhead fixture, a lamp, or screen glow. Outdoors: the sun, sky bounce, or shade. No evidence of reflectors, ring lights, softboxes, or multiple sources. The light wraps around one side of the subject and falls off on the other with minimal fill.",
      "quality": "Soft to moderately directional. You can usually tell where the light is coming from, but the shadows aren't sharp-edged unless the source is direct sun. Fill shadows are dark and unrecovered.",
      "color_temperature": "Warm and inconsistent. The dominant light source sets the warmth — golden window light, warm incandescent bulbs, or natural sun lean amber. Background areas illuminated by secondary sources shift cooler or greener. The auto white balance splits the difference rather than perfectly correcting, leaving subtle color casts across the frame.",
      "dynamic_range": "Narrow. Bright areas and dark areas exist in the same frame but the phone can't hold both — windows blow to white rectangles, sky clips, deep shadows go murky and lose detail. The intended subject sits in the usable middle exposure zone while the extremes get sacrificed.",
      "specular_behavior": "Highlights on shiny surfaces — skin, glass, plastic packaging, polished objects, water, wet surfaces — read as small, intense, slightly irregular catchlights rather than smooth photographic gradients. They clip to flat white patches with no rolloff."
    },

    "subject_and_texture_realism": {
      "skin": "When people are present: visible skin texture at close range — pores, fine lines, slight tonal unevenness, small blemishes, freckles, natural redness in cheeks or nose. Not airbrushed but not exaggerated. The phone's processing smooths slightly but doesn't eliminate. Skin looks alive — slight dewiness in oily zones, matte in dry zones.",
      "hair": "When hair is visible: individual strands visible near the focal area, clumping into softer masses at distance. Flyaways and frizz catch light and glow. Textured hair reads as soft volume rather than defined individual coils at distance. Real movement and slight imperfection rather than salon-styled placement.",
      "fabric_and_materials": "Clothing and textiles show real creasing, wear, slightly rumpled quality — not pressed or steamed. Natural fibers show their weave at close range. Synthetic surfaces show real reflections and scuffs.",
      "objects_and_products": "When products or objects are present, they look like real items in a real space — slight smudges, fingerprints on glass, water droplets, environmental interaction. Not the retouched perfection of a product photography studio. Labels and packaging show real reflections and the slight warping of wide-angle phone lenses.",
      "food_and_liquids": "When food or drinks appear: real condensation, real steam, real crumbs, real imperfect plating. Liquids catch light in genuine ways with small specular highlights, not glycerin-perfect commercial styling."
    },

    "environment_authenticity": {
      "setting": "Lived-in real spaces — bedrooms with unmade beds, kitchens with dishes in the sink, bathrooms with products on the counter, cars with dashboard clutter, cafes with other patrons in the background, streets with real pedestrians and signage, parks with normal park-goers. Nothing is styled or removed for the shot.",
      "depth_separation": "Shallow separation between subject and background but not creamy professional bokeh — more like the background is just slightly less sharp, the way phone portrait modes approximate depth. Some phones show hard-edged masking artifacts where complex shapes (hair, leaves, textured edges) meet the background.",
      "incidental_clutter": "Random real-life objects visible in the frame — chargers, water glasses, crumpled receipts, pillows, hanging plants, jewelry, half-finished drinks, opened packages, pet hair, junk mail. These aren't props; they're incidental details the creator didn't think to remove or didn't care about.",
      "color_palette": "Environments tend toward whatever real spaces actually look like — muted warm neutrals, wood tones, earth-colored textiles, painted walls in real colors, with small pops of uncoordinated color from personal items, brands, and everyday objects. Never a clean studio backdrop.",
      "scale_and_space_cues": "Background objects establish real spatial context — you can sense ceiling height, room size, furniture proximity, the depth of an outdoor scene. The environment reads as a specific, identifiable type of real place (bedroom, car interior, sidewalk, kitchen, bathroom, park bench) rather than an ambiguous void or styled set."
    }
